native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Based on the 1975–2015 WDI group aggregates, the data do not support a larger positive effect of education expenditure on per-capita income for developing (lower-middle-income, LMC) countries than for Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA); if anything, the short-run association is small, positive and statistically indistinguishable from zero for LMC, while the only SSA window in which income is observed (2011–2015, five years) shows a negative association. Concretely, for LMC a one-percentage-point increase in education expenditure as a share of GNI is associated with a same-year change of roughly +20 to +80 constant-2015 US$ in per-capita GNI (about 2–7% of the group's mean per-capita GNI of ~1,180 US$; point estimate +35 US$ in the main autoregressive specification), with none of these estimates statistically distinguishable from zero and a slightly negative (−26 US$/yr) association in first differences. For SSA, per-capita income exists in the data only for 2011–2015, a window in which the education share fell from 3.65% to 3.15% of GNI while income rose 5.1%, yielding an indicative-only negative slope of about −160 to −180 US$ per percentage point. The data-grounded hypothesis is therefore that the effect of education expenditure on per-capita income does not differ in a reliably detectable way between the two groups — neither group exhibits a robust positive effect, and the apparent sign difference (weakly positive for LMC, negative for SSA) is an artifact of the five-year SSA income window rather than a true group difference. Caveats: (i) the file contains GNI per capita in constant 2015 US dollars, not per-capita GDP in 2010 US dollars; (ii) the education series is adjusted savings for education as a percentage of GNI, not government expenditure on education as a percentage of total government expenditure; (iii) the mapping of LMC to 'developing countries' is an interpretive assumption, and the LMC and SSA groups are not mutually exclusive (many SSA countries are lower-middle-income); (iv) with at most 41 LMC group-year observations and only 5 SSA income observations, no formal test of a group difference is feasible and the SSA estimate is highly uncertain; (v) in-sample, the LMC education-expenditure share rose modestly over the full period (2.69 to 3.06 percent of GNI, peaking at 3.87 in 1999) while the SSA share fell (4.30 to 3.15 percent of GNI), so a sustained 'increase in education expenditure' is largely counterfactual in-sample and the estimates should be read as associations, not causal effects.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded and validated worldbank_education_gdp.csv (12 rows = 2 groups x 6 series; 84/492 cells missing, all leading blocks; no duplicates/non-numeric tokens). 2) Pivoted to tidy group-year panels; documented that SSA GNI per capita exists only for 2011-2015 (5 of 41 years) and no imputation was performed. 3) LMC: main ARDL(1,1) with lagged dynamics (n=40, 1976-2015); robustness via first-difference spec (n=39), naive levels (n=40; rejected as spurious, DW=0.26), ARDL + linear time trend diagnostic (n=40), and controls spec 1992-2015 (n=24) with enrollment, labor-force and exports-growth controls plus VIF diagnostics. 4) SSA: bivariate OLS of GNI on lagged (n=4) and concurrent (n=5) education expenditure, inference labelled indicative only. 5) Compared the two slopes side by side in words without any formal difference test; translated the LMC short-run coefficient into a level statement (US$ per capita per +1pp). 6) Drafted the data-grounded natural-language hypothesis with explicit caveats on variable mismatches, the LMC-to-developing-countries mapping, group non-exclusivity, and small-sample limitations; corrected the LMC expenditure-trend description in caveat (v) per reviewer feedback.
